name: Yara Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Harbourside Care, which is a small co-op, so the carers own a share of it. My mornings are four or five calls around the old fishing streets, mostly people with dementia, then a break, then the evening tuck-in calls: meds, a cup of tea, pyjamas, lights. My favourite is my client Mrs Abara, who sings hymns in the shower and tells me off for my haircut. What wears me out is the steps, honestly, those houses are all stairs and no lifts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. The co-op pays a little better than the big agencies on travel, but the hourly rate is still low, and I've got about three weeks' worth saved. My partner Jonas drives the number twelve bus, so between us we cover the rent on our flat above the bakery, just. If either of us lost a week of pay, we'd feel it straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a bit of a relief, if I'm honest. My job's my hands, and I'd rather that didn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the actual problem, which is that care is underfunded. If AI doesn't save the day, the government still has to. I'd probably share something about that at the co-op's members' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means life carries on being tight. The co-op is solid, so I'm not worried about losing my job. I'm worried about the rent going up again in April, because our landlord's already hinted at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and maybe use the chat AI on my phone a bit more, like I already do when I write emails to the council about a client's equipment. I'd ask the co-op about the medication training, because that bumps the hourly rate. And Jonas and I would try to put fifty a month aside before the April rent letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Safe, but like nothing is going to get easier either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the chat AI sometimes. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for letters. Last month I needed to ask the council for a new commode for Mr Petrakis, and the AI helped me write it so it didn't sound like a rant. I checked every word, though. I wouldn't let it near anything about someone's medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the rent goes up in April, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably our car. We share an old one and I mostly walk the rounds anyway. Jonas would hate it, but the bus depot's ten minutes from our flat.

say: I'd say the real problem is that **care is underfunded**, AI or not.
I'd tell the co-op meeting that **government still has to** pay for care properly.
think: I think my **co-op job is safe**, so I'm not scared of losing it.
The worry is a **rent rise in April** that our landlord has already hinted at.
do: Ask the co-op for **medication training**, which raises the hourly rate.
Keep using the **phone chat AI** for letters to the council.
Put **fifty a month** aside with Jonas before the April rent letter.
feel: **Flat**: safe, but nothing is going to get easier.
S0.quote: My job's my hands, and I'd rather that didn't change.
fieldNote: Her job feels **secure in the co-op**, so her worry is rent, not AI.
She already uses AI **carefully for letters**, never for medicine.
She blames **underfunding by government**, consistent with her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Sign up for the co-op's medication training to raise her rate
Save fifty a month with Jonas before the April rent letter
Keep writing council equipment letters with the phone chat AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the paperwork side goes to AI. The co-op office is three people, so that's going to be strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the members' meeting that if AI saves the co-op money on admin, we vote to put it into our wages or longer visits. That's the whole point of a co-op. I'd say it online too, because the big agencies will just pocket it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's mostly good for me. I spend maybe forty minutes a day on care notes. If AI can write my care notes from what I say into my phone, that's forty minutes more a day with people. What worries me is Jonas, because buses are sort of hands-on and sort of not, and nobody really knows when the driverless ones come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the voice-notes tool as soon as the other carers say it works, not before. I'd vote at the co-op for the savings to go into a pay rise. And I'd tell Jonas to look at the bus company's training for the depot workshop, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small knot in my stomach about Jonas, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic, but don't be the last driver on the route either. He's good with engines, so the workshop makes sense. He'd grumble that I'm planning his life, which I am a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the co-op would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhiannon in the office. She does the rota and the invoices, and that's exactly the thinking work on your card. I'd want the co-op to move her onto something like family liaison, because she's brilliant on the phone with worried daughters.

say: I'd say co-op **admin savings** should go to wages or longer visits.
I'd post that **big agencies** will just pocket the savings.
think: I think AI writing care notes gives me **forty minutes more** with people.
I'm more worried about **Jonas's bus job** than my own.
do: Try the **voice-notes tool** once other carers say it works.
Vote at the co-op for savings to fund a **pay rise**.
Urge Jonas to look at the **bus depot workshop** training.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a small knot about **Jonas**.
S1.quote: If AI can write my care notes from what I say into my phone, that's forty minutes more a day with people.
fieldNote: She sees **Steady Disruption** as good for her own hands-on work.
Her worry moves to her **partner's bus job** and the co-op office worker.
She waits for **proof from colleagues** before adopting tools, fitting her steady style.

steps.text: Start using the voice-notes tool once colleagues vouch for it
Vote at the members' meeting to put admin savings into pay
Help Jonas apply for the bus depot workshop training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That one's not a plan, that's a cliff. Robots by 2031, and driverless buses probably too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need a guaranteed income for people whose work disappears, and that care has to stay human by law. I'd join whatever the care workers' union organises, even though the co-op isn't unionised in the usual way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my partner Jonas and I would both be out of work within three years of each other, and we've got three weeks of savings. The co-op's office goes in 2028, which hurts but isn't me. Then in 2031 the robots come for the washing and dressing, and maybe the buses go about then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the nursing associate apprenticeship, because a nurse does more judgement than a carer and maybe lasts longer. I'd cut everything: the car, the phone contracts, the takeaway on Fridays. And I'd ask my mum whether we could move back in with her if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And sort of angry that it would happen to people who were already on the bottom rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the nursing apprenticeship make sense if AI can do thinking work by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I can't answer. A nurse's judgement is thinking work, so the AI might do the decisions and I'd be the hands. But hands still last till 2031, and a nurse's hands get paid more than a carer's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your mum: how would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes before I finished asking, and then she'd tell my aunties. Her place is a two-bedroom flat on the estate behind the school, so Jonas would be on the sofa-bed for a while. It's not a plan I'm proud of, but it's a roof.

say: I'd call for a **guaranteed income** for people whose work disappears.
I'd say care must **stay human by law**, and join union action.
think: I think **both of us** would be out of work within three years.
With **three weeks' savings**, we couldn't last long without wages.
do: Start a **nursing associate apprenticeship** in the first year.
Cut the **car, phone contracts** and Friday takeaway.
Ask her mum about **moving in** if it comes to it.
feel: **Angry** that it hits people already on the bottom rung.
S2.quote: I think my partner Jonas and I would both be out of work within three years of each other, and we've got three weeks of savings.
fieldNote: She treats **both household jobs** as hands-on and both at risk by 2031.
Her plan is to **climb into nursing**, though she sees its thinking part is exposed.
Her fallback is **family**: her mum's two-bedroom flat.

steps.text: Apply for the nursing associate apprenticeship this year
Sell the shared car and cut phone contracts and takeaways
Ask her mum about moving into her flat if needed
Join the care workers' union campaign for a guaranteed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels like enough to actually do something, if we start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before: guaranteed income, care stays human. But I'd also say to other carers, use the time, don't wait for the government to rescue you, because it might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is just enough for a nursing qualification, if I start straight away and my partner Jonas does the cooking. The robots for care come around 2034. So I'd have a few years as a nurse before that. Jonas has the same squeeze, though, and I don't know what he'd move into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the nursing associate apprenticeship next year, while still doing evening calls for the co-op. Jonas and I would put a hundred a month aside instead of fifty. And I'd push the co-op to start a training fund for members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but busy. I'm better when I've got something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doing an apprenticeship plus evening calls: is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For two years, yes, if Jonas cooks. I did a care certificate while working full time when I was twenty-two. It's not fun, but it's doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the extra fifty a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Friday takeaways and my phone upgrade. I've had this cracked screen for a year anyway, I can live with it.

say: I'd repeat my call for a **guaranteed income** and human care.
I'd tell other carers to **use the time** and not wait for rescue.
think: I think five years is just enough for a **nursing qualification**.
Jonas faces the **same squeeze**, and I don't know his next step.
do: Start the **nursing apprenticeship** next year while keeping evening calls.
Raise savings to **a hundred a month** by cutting takeaways.
Push the co-op to create a **members' training fund**.
feel: **Nervous but busy**, which she finds easier to handle.
S3.quote: Five years is just enough for a nursing qualification, if I start straight away and my partner Jonas does the cooking.
fieldNote: With five years, she moves from fear to a **concrete training plan**.
She tells carers not to wait for **government rescue**, a shift from her public line.
Her partner's future is the **unsolved piece**.

steps.text: Begin the nursing associate apprenticeship while doing evening calls
Save a hundred a month by cutting takeaways and the phone upgrade
Propose a members' training fund at the co-op meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a career. You can become something else in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to build a proper public care service, with training and fair pay, before the robots arrive. Ten years is enough for a government to do that if it wants to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be fine. I'd be a qualified nurse well before 2039, and nurses will be the last ones the robots replace on a ward. My worry would be the rent going up every year while I'm studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the nursing associate apprenticeship, then top it up to a full nursing degree part-time. I'd keep two evening calls a week at the co-op for income and because I'd miss Mrs Abara. Jonas would do his workshop training with the bus company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. A bit tired just thinking about the studying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably be fine. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, always money. If the rent jumps or one of us gets ill, the studying stops first. That's happened to people I know at the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI in the studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably like I do with letters, to explain things I don't get from the lecture. Once my friends on the course say it's reliable, anyway. I'd still want a real tutor marking my work.

say: I'd call for a proper **public care service** with training and fair pay.
I'd say ten years is **enough for government** if it wants to act.
think: I think I'd be a **qualified nurse** well before 2039.
My worry would be **yearly rent rises** while I'm studying.
do: Do the **nursing apprenticeship**, then a part-time nursing degree.
Keep **two evening calls** a week at the co-op for income.
Use AI to **explain course material**, once classmates say it's reliable.
feel: **Hopeful**, though tired thinking about years of study.
S4.quote: Ten years is a career. You can become something else in ten years.
fieldNote: A decade turns her plan into a **realistic career change** into nursing.
Money stays the **weak point**: rent or illness could stop her studies.
She keeps a **personal tie** to a favourite client while retraining.

steps.text: Complete the nursing apprenticeship, then a part-time nursing degree
Keep two co-op evening calls a week for income
Use a study AI for course questions once classmates trust it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Jonas and I would both be on the same cliff edge at the same time. What would help is free, paid training for care workers to become nurses, and some kind of income guarantee so we're not choosing between studying and rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who looks after the carers. Nobody asks if care workers are okay, and we're the ones climbing everybody's stairs.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks if care workers are okay, and we're the ones climbing everybody's stairs.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old carer** at a small coastal care co-op, specialising in clients with dementia.
She has about **three weeks' savings** and shares rent with her partner Jonas, a bus driver.
She feels her own job is safe in mild worlds, but **both incomes** are at risk with AGI.
Her answer to every faster scenario is **training** to become a **nurse**, plus cutting costs.
She is **progressive**, blaming underfunding and calling for guaranteed income and public care.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and Jonas facing job loss at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Free, paid training** for care workers to become nurses.
An **income guarantee** so she isn't choosing between study and rent.
